lead: Work and heat are not things stored inside a system. They are energy transfers across a boundary, and each is counted only while the transfer happens. A boundary that blocks heat is adiabatic; one that lets heat cross is diathermic. Before calculation, fix one sign convention. Here, heat entering a system is positive (Q > 0), and work done by the system is positive (W > 0). The surroundings see the opposite signs. This is the language of engines, refrigerators and power plants, where the direction of energy flow decides whether it is useful output or a cost.
prereq: You need: 1.2 for system and boundary, and 1.4 for equilibrium and quasi-static paths.

blocks.text: Work is energy transfer by a force moving its point of application. In thermodynamics the force often comes from a pressure on a moving boundary; other modes, such as shaft work and electrical work, follow the same pattern. Work has symbol W and unit joule (J); 1 kJ = 1000 J. Work is not a property stored in the system. It exists only while the force acts and the boundary moves.

blocks.where: F is force in N, x is displacement of the point of application in m, and W is work in J.

blocks.text: Heat is energy transfer because of a temperature difference between system and surroundings. Heat has symbol Q and unit J or kJ. A hot vessel in a cooler room loses heat; the energy crossing is Q, not a property called heat inside the vessel. Heat transfer stops when temperatures equal. Small amounts are written δQ and δW; Q and W themselves are path functions, not state properties (1.3). Some syllabi call these heat and work interactions. Both are boundary phenomena: choose the boundary first, then Q and W have meaning.

sections.h3: Sign convention used in this book

blocks.text: Take heat entering the system as positive: Q > 0. Take work done by the system on the surroundings as positive: W > 0. Then Q < 0 means heat leaves the system, and W < 0 means work is done on the system. The surroundings get the opposite signs, because a transfer out of the system is a transfer into the surroundings. Engineering texts often use this convention because engines and turbines produce work; a positive W is useful output. Fix the convention before substituting numbers. A statement such as W = −20 kJ is meaningless until you say which side is positive.
Q = Q_in − Q_out,   W = W_out − W_in
blocks.where: Q_in is heat entering in kJ, Q_out is heat leaving in kJ, W_out is work done by the system in kJ, and W_in is work done on the system in kJ.

blocks.text: The combination Q − W appears in the worked example as the net transfer into the system; Unit 2 connects it to internal energy.

An adiabatic boundary blocks heat transfer: Q = 0 across it. A thermos flask and a thick insulated steam pipe are approximations. Adiabatic does not mean isolated; work can still cross, and mass can cross if the boundary is open. An isolated system has no heat, no work and no mass crossing (1.2). A diathermic boundary allows heat transfer, but it does not force it. A metal wall between two regions at the same temperature is diathermic and still has Q = 0. The word tells you what may cross, not what does cross in a given process. A movable boundary lets displacement work cross; a rigid boundary blocks it. Check both labels: thermal (adiabatic or diathermic) and mechanical (rigid or movable).

Q and W depend on the path between the same two states. Heat a gas slowly at constant pressure, or heat it quickly and let the pressure change; the end states can match while Q and W differ. This is why Q and W are not properties and why a table of properties cannot list them. It is also why the sign convention must be written at the top of a solution. If a problem says “work done on the system is 20 kJ” and your convention is W > 0 for work by the system, enter W = −20 kJ. If it says “heat rejected is 30 kJ”, enter Q = −30 kJ. State the convention, convert each phrase to a signed number, then calculate. Do not change the convention halfway.

examples.question: A closed system receives 50 kJ of heat from a hot reservoir and does 20 kJ of work on the surroundings. Take heat added to the system as positive and work done by the system as positive. (a) Write Q and W with signs. (b) Find the net energy transfer Q − W.
steps: Choose the convention: Q > 0 for heat into the system; W > 0 for work by the system on the surroundings.
Heat received: 50 kJ enters, so Q = +50 kJ.
Work done by the system: 20 kJ leaves as work, so W = +20 kJ.
Substitute: Q − W = (+50 kJ) − (+20 kJ) = +30 kJ.
The positive result means net energy enters the system by these two interactions: 30 kJ.
examples.answer: Q = +50 kJ, W = +20 kJ, and Q − W = +30 kJ.
examples.check:
Q_kJ = 50.0
W_kJ = 20.0
net_kJ = Q_kJ - W_kJ
print(Q_kJ)
print(W_kJ)
print(net_kJ)

traps: Using W > 0 for work done on the system without saying so. In the convention here, work done on the system is W = −20 kJ, not +20 kJ.
Treating heat as a property stored in the system. Q is energy crossing the boundary; internal energy is the property, covered in Unit 2.
Writing Q = +30 kJ for “30 kJ of heat rejected”. Rejected heat leaves the system, so Q = −30 kJ in this convention.
Confusing adiabatic with isolated. An adiabatic boundary has Q = 0; an isolated system also has W = 0 and no mass crossing.
Forgetting units in the sign statement. A number like W = 20 is incomplete; write W = +20 kJ and state the convention.

quiz.q: State the sign convention for Q and W used in this book.
quiz.a: Q > 0 when heat enters the system; W > 0 when work is done by the system on the surroundings.

quiz.q: Why are Q and W called path functions rather than properties?
quiz.a: Their values depend on how the system moves between states; the same end states can have different Q and W. Properties depend only on state.

quiz.q: What does a diathermic boundary allow, and does it always transfer heat?
quiz.a: It allows heat transfer. It does not force heat transfer; Q can be zero if temperatures are equal.

quiz.q: A system rejects 25 kJ of heat and receives 10 kJ of work. Using Q > 0 into the system and W > 0 by the system, write Q and W.
quiz.a: Heat rejected: Q = −25 kJ. Work received by the system: W = −10 kJ.

quiz.q: A system takes in 80 kJ of heat and does 35 kJ of work. Find Q − W with the book convention.
quiz.a: Q = +80 kJ, W = +35 kJ, so Q − W = +45 kJ.

quiz.q: A closed system has an adiabatic boundary and a movable piston. Can it exchange work? Can it exchange heat? What is Q?
quiz.a: Yes, work can cross through the moving piston. No heat crosses the adiabatic boundary, so Q = 0.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, the sign convention is built into software for heat exchangers and turbines, where a negative duty means heat removal. In research, calorimeters measure Q by temperature change, while dynamometers measure shaft work, and both must report signs explicitly. Newer curricula often add exergy accounting, where a transfer of heat at low temperature is worth less than the same number of joules of work. Search for “thermodynamic sign convention heat work”, “adiabatic boundary”, and “diathermic boundary”.
